key_findings.detail:
Stacking faults (SFs) in silicon are extrinsic planar defects on {111} crystal planes:

- Penetrate **> 1 µm into silicon**, completely crossing the p-n junction depth (~200–300 nm from surface)
- Burgers vector: **a/3[111]** (extrinsic stacking fault, ESF)
- Thin Na-decorated layer: only **a few tenths of a nanometer** thick, but sufficient to create an ohmic channel
- HAADF STEM imaging confirms a dark region (Na accumulation) within the defect plane; this dark region disappears after thermal recovery, confirming reversibility

- [[papers/Wiley-311-3837-2-s2.0-84939654596-2015-J-Nanoscopic studies of 2D-extended defects in silicon that cause shunting of Si-solar cells.pdf#page=2|Naumann et al. (2015), p.2]]

key_findings.claim: Na Area Density Required for Shunting
key_findings.detail:
Na⁺ decoration creates a highly conductive metallic-like channel:

- Na area density within the stacking fault plane: **$\sim 10^{15}$ cm$^{-2}$**
- This density creates a shunt conductivity: $\sigma_{sf}(t) \propto n(0,t)$, where $n$ is the Na concentration at the stacking fault center
- Shunt resistance relationship: $1/R_{sh} = \sigma_0 + \sigma_{sf}(t)$

- [[papers/IEEE-164-2299-2-s2.0-85087499813-2020-J-A Drift and Diffusion Model for PID-s in Solar Modules.pdf#page=3|Schulze et al. (2020), p.3]]
- [[papers/Wiley-311-3837-2-s2.0-84939654596-2015-J-Nanoscopic studies of 2D-extended defects in silicon that cause shunting of Si-solar cells.pdf#page=3|Naumann et al. (2015), p.3]]

The collapse of shunt resistance is the primary measurable indicator of stacking fault shunting:

- **Before PID:** Rsh ~ 1000 Ω (module level)
- **After 48 h severe PID (−1000 V, 85°C/85% RH):** Rsh ~ 2 Ω — a **500× reduction** to 0.2% of original
- After 491 days natural recovery: Rsh = 18.1 Ω (still only 1.8% of original; incomplete recovery)
- [[papers/Other-81-1747-2-s2.0-85129456088-2022-other-Monitoring the natural recovery of potential induced degradation in poly-crystalline photovoltaic mo.pdf#page=3|Kwembur et al. (2022), p.3]]

At the cell level (multicrystalline Si, 85°C, 1000 V, 1.5 h):
- Rsh drops from 10+ kΩ to effectively 0 (full shunting)
- EL images show complete blackout of entire cell area by 2.5 h
- [[papers/Elsevier-541-3483-2-s2.0-84991699729-2016-J-Microscopic aspects of potential induced degradation phenomena and their recovery processes for p ty.pdf#page=4|Luo et al. (2016), p.4]]

key_findings.claim: Spatial Distribution of Shunts: EL Imaging
key_findings.detail:
Electroluminescence (EL) imaging is the primary diagnostic for stacking fault shunts:

- Dark areas expand in EL images starting from corners/edges (high field regions) and spreading inward
- Dark areas correlate with shunt locations and reduced photocurrent generation
- In cells where Na was applied to a half-area: dark areas expand from the application point and cover the entire cell over 6–7 h
- [[papers/Elsevier-541-3483-2-s2.0-84991699729-2016-J-Microscopic aspects of potential induced degradation phenomena and their recovery processes for p ty.pdf#page=3|Luo et al. (2016), p.3]]

Na-decorated stacking faults are partially or fully reversible through Na out-diffusion:

- **Natural recovery (dark, open-circuit, room temperature):** Pmax recovers to 95.6% after 487 days (moderate PID) or 62.8% after 491 days (severe PID)
- **Thermal annealing / positive voltage application:** Complete recovery of Rsh requires ~2500 h at 90°C; full cell performance recovers faster (before Rsh fully recovers)
- **After recovery:** Remaining extrinsic stacking fault (without Na) shows **no conductivity** — confirming the stacking fault itself is not the shunt; Na decoration is essential

- [[papers/IEEE-164-2299-2-s2.0-85087499813-2020-J-A Drift and Diffusion Model for PID-s in Solar Modules.pdf#page=5|Schulze et al. (2020), p.5]]
- [[papers/Other-81-1747-2-s2.0-85129456088-2022-other-Monitoring the natural recovery of potential induced degradation in poly-crystalline photovoltaic mo.pdf#page=4|Kwembur et al. (2022), p.4]]

Not all PID-induced shunts are equivalent in recovery potential:

- **Non-ohmic shunts:** Higher recovery potential (surface recombination effects, reversible)
- **Ohmic shunts:** Limited recovery potential (structural Na⁺ incorporation, often irreversible); ~10–40% of severely PID-affected cells show permanent ohmic shunts
- [[papers/Wiley-58-403-2-s2.0-105002608539-2025-J-Identification of Recoverable and Non-Recoverable Potential-Induced Degradation-Shunted Cells in Cry.pdf#page=4|Kumar & Gupta (2025), p.4]]
